abstract: An image-processing framework for detecting exoplanets directly has been developed. The technique overcomes the telescope-stability barrier that has limited previous methods, reveals fainter exoplanets than other approaches can detect and could make imaging exo-Earths easier for future observatories. A physics-based model enables the observation of exoplanets that were undetectable using standard techniques.
title: Faint exoplanets detected using computational approach to remove glare from stars

abstract: The duration of short ångström-wavelength X-ray pulses, which lasted merely 170 attoseconds, has finally been measured accurately. The optical system designed for precision pulse duration metrology can be used as a ‘stopwatch’ to measure the rapid motion of electrons inside atoms and molecules, too. Short pulses generated by the system could be used to observe electrons moving around atomic nuclei.
title: X-ray stopwatch can measure durations of just attoseconds

abstract: Abstract Germanic languages, including German, English, Frisian, Dutch and the Nordic languages, are widely spoken across northwest Europe. However, the timing and location of the prehistoric arrival of this Indo-European linguistic phylum, as well as its Iron Age diversification, remain contentious 1–3 . Here, by sequencing 712 ancient human genomes and analysing them alongside 4,009 previously published genomes, we identify an archaeologically elusive population that entered Sweden, likely from the Baltic region, by around 4000 bp . This population, which became widespread throughout Scandinavia by 3500 bp , offers a potential vector for the introduction of the Germanic language group to Scandinavia 4–6 , some 800 years later than traditionally assumed 7–9 . Following the Late Iron Age disintegration of Germanic into its descendant languages, we observe by 1650 bp a southward migration from southern Scandinavia into presumed Celtic-speaking areas, including present-day Germany, Poland and the Netherlands. During the subsequent Migration Period (1575–1375 bp ), we see this ancestry among Germanic-speaking Anglo-Saxons in Britain and Langobards in southern Europe. In the same time period, we identify a related large-scale northward back-migration into Denmark and southern Sweden, coinciding with the rise of Danish influence and the linguistically documented emergence of Old Norse. These findings indicate that multiple migrations and geographical locations had a major role in the arrival and formation of Germanic, as well as in its divergence into historical and modern descendant languages.
title: Tracing the spread of Germanic languages using ancient genomics

abstract: Abstract Fibrous materials, ranging from connective tissues 1–4 to engineered composites 5–8 , are vital to many biological and man-made systems, optimized to withstand complex in operando or in vivo loading. The load-bearing capacity of intervertebral discs (IVDs) of the spine depends on a hierarchical extracellular matrix, where plywood-like lamellae of collagen fibres in the annulus fibrosus contain nanometre-scale fibrils built from staggered triple-helical monomers 4,9,10 . How intact IVDs couple fibril-scale mechanics to fibre-scale organization under load remains unresolved. Here we introduce TomoSAXS, a full-field 3D small-angle X-ray scattering tomography that maps fibril-to-fibre mechanics across an intact tissue. We show that intrafibrillar molecular pre-strain (D-period stagger) is lamellar textured and tightly correlated with microscale fibre strain. Pre-strain is inversely related to fibril strain and its variability, consistent with load-sharing through molecular unwinding. Radial strain bridges and high-curvature zones at the annulus fibrosus–nucleus pulposus interfaces emerge as critical regulators of local mechanics. These findings reveal concerted fibril–fibre interactions that sustain mechanical equilibrium in the IVD, preserving elasticity and shape. More broadly, TomoSAXS establishes a platform to visualize nanoscale-to-microscale matrix mechanics across biological and synthetic fibrous materials, with applications in ageing and disease, therapeutic evaluation and the design of bio-based and bio-inspired materials.
title: Multimodal X-ray imaging reveals hierarchical fibre mechanics

abstract: Abstract The Great Unconformity marks a globally extensive erosive surface linked to climatic shifts 1 and environmental transitions 2 that preceded the Cambrian explosion of life. The processes proposed to explain the formation of the Great Unconformity include glacial erosion during the Snowball Earth 1,3,4 , rifting and plume activity 5–7 , sea-level fall 8 and mantle-driven dynamic topography 6,9–11 . However, the dynamics of these processes have not been tested. Here we show that continental-scale uplift and subsidence associated with long-wavelength dynamic topography 12 due to mantle convection drove the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity. Our models predict prolonged continental-scale Neoproterozoic uplift and long-term Phanerozoic subsidence for Laurentia, Baltica and North China. This vertical motion scenario is ideal for the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity, which is a first-order surface expression of deep Earth processes. The predicted prolonged continental uplift throughout Cryogenian times would have resulted in marked erosion due to the action of glaciers 13 . The large area of Laurentia and limited deformation at its margins explain why the Great Unconformity is best preserved and documented there. Our models predict cycles of dynamic topography that are broadly reflected in preserved sediment volume across continents 1,14 , and open new avenues for understanding the environments of Cambrian animal diversification.
title: The deep Earth origin of the Great Unconformity

abstract: Abstract Glioblastoma is incurable and resistant to therapy despite genomic stability under treatment 1–8 , suggesting that non-genetic cellular plasticity is a central driver of progression. Whether such plasticity reflects stochastic state switching or is governed by predictable gene regulation has remained unclear 9–13 . Here we introduce scDORI (single-cell deep multi-omic regulatory inference)—a deep-learning framework that infers enhancer-driven gene-regulatory networks at single-cell resolution—and apply it to single-nucleus multiome profiles of more than one million cells from primary glioblastomas. Integrating computational inference with systematic perturbation screens across patient-derived models, we show that a structured regulatory program with an asymmetric interplay of activators and repressors governs cellular plasticity in glioblastoma. The resulting transition landscape is hierarchical and predictable, but permits cross-lineage trajectories that are absent from normal neurodevelopment. Within this landscape, low-plasticity states such as the neuronal-like state are not stable differentiation end points but actively maintained configurations, stabilized by a network of safeguard repressors that silence alternative fates. We identify MYT1L as the dominant member of this network, and show that it binds to and represses master regulators of every alternative state to consolidate neuronal-like identity. MYT1L restricted plasticity even under standard-of-care therapy and suppressed tumour growth and invasion in vivo. Conversely, loss of MYT1L reactivated plasticity and accelerated malignant features, indicating that low-plasticity identity requires continuous repression. These findings reframe malignant cell state stability as a balance between activation and continuous repression, and nominate safeguard repressors as candidate therapeutic targets that are distinct from differentiation-inducing activators, with potential relevance across cancers in which phenotypic switching drives therapy resistance.
title: Decoding the regulatory programs governing glioblastoma plasticity

abstract: Abstract Celtic languages are today restricted to Europe’s Atlantic fringes but were widely spoken across the continent during the Iron Age 1–3 . How Celtic achieved this early distribution remains contested 4 , with alternative archaeological and linguistic models proposing different homelands and dispersal routes. Here we analyse genome-wide data from 4,587 ancient individuals, focusing on Bronze and Iron Age Europe, to test the extent to which these models fit reconstructed demographic histories. We identify three main processes shaping European population structure that are relevant to the Celtic dispersal. First, the arrival of Steppe-related ancestry with Bell Beaker-associated groups after around 4400 bp (calibrated years before present or 1950 ce ) across the region in which Celtic and related languages were later spoken. Second, a movement from southwestern Europe into Britain during the Bronze Age (3800–3200 bp ), consistent with scenarios in which Celtic formed along the Atlantic façade. Third, a westward expansion of ancestry related to Late Bronze Age Knovíz–Urnfield-associated populations from eastern central Europe (3200–2800 bp ), affecting France, the British Isles, northeastern Iberia and Italy and later associated with Iron Age Hallstatt and La Tène contexts 5–8 . Although all three movements have parallels with proposed models, we argue that the final movement, from eastern central Europe, is most parsimonious for the spread of Celtic. Although human history does not necessarily follow a parsimonious trajectory 9 and language shifts need not track genetic change, these results delimit the demographic scenarios that are plausible for the emergence of Celtic in prehistoric Europe.
title: Tracing the spread of Celtic languages using ancient genomics

abstract: Abstract Mating decisions are often attributed to the sensory signalling between prospective sexual partners. Yet these interactions are also shaped by the broader environmental context in which they unfold, to appropriately align sexual arousal with reproductive opportunities 1–6 . Here we show that in Drosophila erecta mating is strictly contingent on the ecological and social environment generated as flies densely aggregate in groups on a food patch. We find that food volatiles directly promote male sexual arousal, triggering individuals to sample and pursue potential mates, giving rise to dynamic interactions across the group. The ensuing visual motion transforms each male’s visual field, which in turn further amplifies his arousal, generating a multisensory feedback loop that coordinately promotes courtship across individuals. D. erecta ’s strict dependence on environmental cues appears latent in related species, such as Drosophila melanogaster , where food odour can promote arousal 7 but is dispensable for vigorous courtship. Comparative circuit analyses show that species-specific thresholds for sexual arousal reflect variation in how olfactory input modulates conserved nodes controlling courtship drive, rendering food volatiles a strict sensory gate only in D. erecta . Together, our findings highlight how environmental cues not directly tied to sexual signalling can profoundly influence reproductive behaviour and reorganize the social landscape to ensure mating occurs in contexts where reproductive opportunities are abundant.
title: Ecological and social cues orchestrate concerted courtship in Drosophila

abstract: Abstract Mycobacterium tuberculosis , the causative agent of tuberculosis, remains the world’s deadliest pathogen 1 . Despite intensive study, many of its genes remain uncharacterized, which limits the insight that can be gained into tuberculosis biology and constrains drug development. Genetic interaction (GI) mapping is a powerful strategy to define functional relationships between genes by quantifying how the phenotypic effects of combined perturbations deviate from expectations based on single-gene perturbations 2,3 . Here we develop a dual-sgRNA CRISPR-interference platform that enables high-throughput GI mapping in mycobacteria. We address key technical challenges in library construction and data interpretation by incorporating unique barcodes for each sgRNA pair and implementing a robust statistical pipeline for GI detection. Focusing on essential genes, we generate comprehensive GI maps in the model mycobacterium Mycobacterium smegmatis and the pathogen M. tuberculosis . These maps recapitulate known biology, uncover thousands of previously unrecognized interactions and identify functional connections between essential genes and drug targets. By generating AlphaFold3-based protein–protein interaction predictions 4 for all gene pairs in our GI maps, we show that a subset of GIs is likely to reflect underlying physical associations. Validation of selected GIs confirms both novel biological relationships and opportunities for synergistic targeting. Overall, this work establishes a generalizable framework for dual-gene perturbation and defines the architecture of essential-gene networks in mycobacteria, advancing both our understanding of tuberculosis biology and the rational design of combination therapies.
title: Comprehensive mapping of essential-gene interactions in M. tuberculosis

abstract: Abstract Exoplanet imaging is the main method for detailed characterization of planets orbiting beyond 1 au (ref. 1 ) but it requires suppressing the bright glare of the star to see the faint planet light. As well as sophisticated instrumentation 2,3 , effective image processing is necessary for starlight suppression, which continues to be a substantial limitation 4 . Standard algorithms use reference images for starlight modelling and thus they are limited by inevitable telescope instabilities that change from reference to science observation 5,6 . Addressing this challenge will increase the number of planets amenable to direct imaging and will be a notable step towards imaging exo-Earths with future observatories 7 . Here we present a new physics-based method for starlight subtraction. Our method combines a multistep optimization with a flexible physical model to produce a starlight model, allowing modelling and compensation of instrument instabilities. We use automatic differentiation (autodiff) 8 to optimize millions of model parameters. We demonstrate our method on observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) Near-InfraRed Camera (NIRCam) 9–11 coronagraph instrument. We achieve sensitivity 2–15 times superior to standard techniques, including the first detection of 51 Eridani b (ref. 12 ) at 4.3 μm. This is the first time, to our knowledge, that such an approach has demonstrated substantially improved sensitivity on real, on-sky coronagraphic imaging. Our framework can be extended to other current and future ground-based and space-based observatories, including the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO), potentially relaxing the unprecedented stability requirements needed to make these a success.
title: Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit

abstract: ABSTRACT The ability to observe the social behavior of others and use observed information to bias future action is a fundamental building block of social cognition 1,2 . A foundational question is whether social observation and experience engage common circuit mechanisms that enable behavioral change. While classic studies on social learning have shown that aggressive behaviors can be learned through observation 3 , it remains unclear whether aggression observation promotes persistent neural changes that generalize to new contexts. Here, to directly compare the effects of aggression experience and observation at brain-wide scale, we develop a strategy to perform large-scale cell-type specific recordings across subcortical networks for social behavior control and learning. We record longitudinally while animals “train” through direct experience or observation, then probe shared differences in behavior and neural activity in a novel “hard” aggression context. Using supervised and unsupervised methods for behavioral quantification, we detect unique signatures of a shared behavioral strategy not present in animals with no training. During observation, we find widespread activation that mimics experience in networks for behavior generation, with critical differences in signals associated with reward and threat learning. After observation, we observe that changes persist into the novel aggression context, with increased similarity in the neural dynamics between experience and observation groups. Network-level modeling reveals persistent shared changes to a core aggression network, with widespread decoupling of inhibition from a key hypothalamic output region. This demonstrates that “experience-like” activity during observation can recruit a shared plasticity mechanism that biases behavior toward adaptive defensive strategies in new contexts.
title: Aggression experience and observation drive shared behavioural and neural changes

abstract: Abstract The importance of the gut microbiome in human health has been widely recognized, with alterations in species abundances now reported for many different diseases. In recent years, observations of within-species genetic diversity and strain-level functional differences have urged the field to transition to analyzing microbes at the genetic level, taking advantage of genetic variants in the metagenome to pinpoint relevant genes and pathways. Here, we conducted a phenome-wide association study (PheWAS) of 12.7 million gut microbial single nucleotide variants (SNVs) with 244 host health phenotypes and environmental exposures in 10,781 individuals from six independent cohorts from Europe and Africa. We found 3,018 associations supported by at least two cohorts for 105 host factors, including age, sex and cardiovascular and metabolic parameters. Moreover, we found 34,927 significant associations in single-cohort analyses where SNV–phenotype pairs were only available for one cohort. All identified associations are detailed in an online catalog (https://fulab.web.rug.nl/SNV-MWAS/). The associated microbial SNVs inform mechanistic hypotheses about microbial functionality in human health and provide insights into microbial adaptation and evolution in response to changes in the environment and host physiology. For example, we identified 718 age-associated gut microbial SNVs across multiple cohorts and used these microbial SNVs to accurately predict host age. We also identified SNVs in microbial genes associated with lipid concentrations and BMI, including SNVs in the isoleucine-tRNA synthetase gene of Clostridium phoceensis and an α-Melanocyte-stimulating hormone-mimicking clpB gene of Alistipes ihumii. Mediation analysis provided evidence that microbial genetic variations may be under selection enforced by environmental factors, but also that they mediate the effects on the host, e.g. the isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase gene of C. phoceensis mediated dietary effects on four phenotypes. Overall, this study identifies new biological connections between human host and microbial genetic variants, exposing the functional layer of gut microbiome data hidden at base pair resolution and revealing microbial adaptation and evolution in relation to host lifestyle and physiology.
title: Microbiome-wide PheWAS links gut microbial SNVs to health and exposures

abstract: Abstract The VEGF ligand and its main receptor VEGFR2 are considered to be essential for endothelial differentiation, proliferation, sprouting and survival. Blood vessels cannot form in growing embryos or tissues when VEGF/VEGFR2 signalling is compromised in all cells. The Anti-VEGF blocking antibody is one of the most widely used antibodies in the clinics, blocking angiogenesis in cancer, wound healing or in ischemic diseases. However, vascular resistance to Anti-VEGF has been reported. Here we used iFlpMosaics and iSuRe-HadCre to induce and track genetic mosaics of endothelial cells (ECs) lacking VEGFR2 during the entire embryonic and postnatal development. Surprisingly, Vegfr2 KO ECs adapt, proliferate normally and compete with wild-type cells over time, ultimately forming a substantial portion of the capillary network in most organs. We found that Vegfr2 KO ECs are not able to sprout during the first wave of angiogenesis in most tissues, because it is highly VEGF-dependent and favours the growth and mobilization of wild-type ECs. However, due to their inability to respond to VEGF, over time Vegfr2 KO ECs become dominant in veins, which provide for a long term and continuous source of ECs for subsequent waves of VEGF-independent angiogenesis. Comparative scRNAseq analysis of ECs with acute and long-term loss of VEGFR2, revealed both common and organ-specific molecular mechanisms of adaptation and resistance to VEGF signalling loss. This included significant endothelial venousization and the upregulation of ligands for VEGFR1 and VEGFR3. VEGFR1 only partially compensated for VEGFR2 loss in capillary ECs, whereas VEGFR3 only compensated in arterial ECs. Loss of the three VEGF receptors did not compromise venous growth. This work changes our understanding of the role of VEGF signaling and its receptors in angiogenesis and reveals mechanisms of adaptation and resistance to their loss.
title: Venousization enables angiogenesis in the absence of VEGFR signalling

abstract: Abstract Cancer cells display highly heterogeneous and plastic states in glioblastoma, an incurable brain tumour. However, how these malignant states arise and whether they follow defined cellular trajectories across tumours is poorly understood. Here, we generated a deep single cell and spatial multi-omic atlas of human glioblastoma that pairs transcriptomic, epigenomic and genomic profiling of 12 tumours across multiple regions. We identify that glioblastoma heterogeneity is driven by spatially-patterned transitions of cancer cells from developmental-like states towards those defined by a glial injury response and hypoxia. This cellular trajectory regionalises tumours into distinct tissue niches and manifests in a molecularly conserved manner across tumours as well as genetically distinct tumour subclones. Moreover, using a new deep learning framework to map cancer cell states jointly with clones in situ , we show that tumour subclones are finely spatially intermixed through glioblastoma tissue niches. Finally, we show that this cancer cell trajectory is intimately linked to myeloid heterogeneity and unfolds across regionalised myeloid signalling environments. Our findings define a stereotyped trajectory of cancer cells in glioblastoma and unify glioblastoma tumour heterogeneity into a tractable cellular and tissue framework.
title: A spatiotemporal cancer cell trajectory underlies glioblastoma heterogeneity

abstract: ABSTRACT Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is highly heritable, and mutations in hundreds of genes have been implicated as individually rare causes of ASD 1–3 . Understanding how disruptions to these functionally diverse genes lead to the core features of ASD remains a major challenge 4 . Moreover, ASD is three- to four-fold more common in males than females 5 , and autistic females tend to carry more autosomal risk alleles for ASD compared to autistic males 6,7 , but the biological basis of this “female protective effect” (FPE) is unknown 8,9 . Here we show that individual perturbations of 18 ASD genes in human neural progenitor cells converge on shared effects on gene expression, including widespread downregulation of other ASD genes. De novo reconstruction of a gene regulatory network (GRN) enabled the identification of central transcriptional regulators, including the prominent ASD gene CHD8 as well as novel candidates such as REST , that drive this transcriptomic convergence. Furthermore, the X-linked transcription factor ZFX , which is expressed from both the active and the inactive X chromosomes in females 10 , emerged as a key activator of many ASD genes: we propose that the higher ZFX expression level observed in female brain can buffer damaging mutations in diverse ASD genes, contributing to the FPE. Together, these results reveal how key GRNs can become broadly and similarly dysregulated upon disruption of individual ASD genes and provide molecular insight into the female protective effect in ASD.
title: Transcriptomic convergence and the female protective effect in autism

abstract: Abstract Hydrogen-bearing materials are central to low-carbon energy technologies 1 , but hydrogen itself is difficult to detect and localize at the nanoscale 2–6 . This hinders the development of advanced materials with better efficiency. Atom probe tomography (APT) can map hydrogen in three dimensions and at high resolution, yet characterization of dilute, mobile, interstitial hydrogen in metals has remained challenging because of low solubility, the ambiguity owing to hydrogen trapping by structural defects, as well as the artefacts introduced during hydrogen introduction 4–6 . Here we address whether interstitial hydrogen in solution in materials can be distinguished from defect-trapped hydrogen in APT. Using deuterium as a proxy for hydrogen, together with face-centred cubic (FCC) multi-principal-element alloys (MPEAs) containing coherent FCC precipitates, we show that deuterium atoms reproducibly concentrate in hydrogen-affinitive phases in a manner consistent with theoretical predictions. We further resolve differences in deuterium content between phases with distinct local chemistries and crystal structures, consistent with their different calculated hydrogen solution energies. These findings demonstrate that APT can move beyond identifying hydrides and solute-decorated defects to examine hydrogen in solid solution, providing new insights into hydrogen partitioning in structural alloys and informing materials design for hydrogen-related applications.
title: Towards observing interstitial hydrogen in solution in metal lattices

abstract: Algal blooms are hotspots for diverse microbial interactions affecting bloom dynamics. Viral infections often regulate the demise of these blooms, recycling >25% of oceanic fixed carbon. Although these blooms collapse synchronously, only 10-30% of algal cells show active viral infection, suggesting additional mortality agents. Using microbial communities from natural coccolithophore blooms, we discovered that bacteria significantly enhanced virus-mediated algal mortality. We quantified this interaction using two novel metrics: the Synergy Index (SI) measuring viral-bacterial interaction strength, and the Benefit Index (BI) assessing changes in bacterial fitness. We identified Alteromonas bacteria as drivers of viral-bacterial coinfection, with consistently high SI and BI. In natural communities, Alteromonas exhibited chemoattraction towards infected algal cells, leading to their enrichment in bloom demise particles. This viral-bacterial synergy represents a previously unrecognized mortality agent controlling bloom termination, modulating the balance between the carbon-recycling viral shunt and the carbon-exporting viral shuttle pathways, likely influencing global carbon cycling.
title: Synergy in viral–bacterial co-infection expedites algal bloom demise

abstract: Abstract Rubella virus (RuV) causes rubella and, when acquired during pregnancy, congenital rubella syndrome (CRS). Despite its clinical significance, the cellular entry mechanism of RuV remains poorly characterized owing to limited knowledge of host receptors, hampering pathogenesis studies and therapeutic development. Here, we identify Nectin-4 as a functional RuV entry receptor through proximity biotin labeling-based proteomics coupled with CRISPR/Cas9 validation. Notably, Nectin-4 is shared with measles virus, revealing convergent evolution in viral entry despite the different viral families. Nectin-4 directly interacts with the RuV envelope glycoproteins through its ectodomain, facilitating receptor-mediated endocytosis following initial calcium-dependent viral attachment. In polarized respiratory epithelial cells, Nectin-4 mediates basolateral viral entry and subsequent apical release of progeny virions, enabling efficient respiratory transmission. Using human placental organoid models, we demonstrate that syncytiotrophoblasts serve as primary targets for transplacental RuV infection, with viral entry significantly inhibited by Nectin-4 blockade. These findings establish Nectin-4 as critical for both horizontal respiratory transmission and vertical maternal–fetal transmission of RuV. Our results provide fundamental insights into RuV pathogenesis and identify Nectin-4 as a promising therapeutic target for CRS. Importantly, the discovery of shared receptor utilization between RuV and measles virus opens new avenues for integrated elimination strategies targeting both pathogens.
title: Nectin-4 mediates rubella virus entry in airway and placental cells

abstract: The activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome necessitates its aggregation within the dispersed trans-Golgi network (dTGN) and subsequent transport from the dTGN to the microtubule organizing center (MTOC), a process facilitated by HDAC6. However, the regulatory mechanisms governing the formation of NLRP3 aggregates remain insufficiently understood. In this study, we demonstrate that proteasome impairment induces polyubiquitination and aggregation of NLRP3 at the MTOC. We demonstrate ubiquitin-specific protease 46 (USP46) as a key factor that recognizes NLRP3 as a substrate and restricts nondegradative K63-linked polyubiquitination at lysine residue K930, thereby preventing excessive aggregation, transport to the MTOC, and inflammasome activation. Furthermore, myeloid-specific knockout of USP46 exacerbates renal injury and inflammation in both lipopolysaccharide-induced-induced endotoxic shock and pristane-induced lupus nephritis models. Our findings provide insights into the regulatory mechanisms underlying the aggresomal activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: USP46 restrains K63-linked polyubiquitination–dependent aggregation and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in lupus nephritis

abstract: Abstract The tight regulation of the integrin family of extracellular matrix (ECM) receptors is essential for the coordination of most cellular processes. Talin regulates integrin function by binding to the cytoplasmic tail of the integrin beta subunit. Two integrin-binding sites (IBS) in talin have been reported, one in the talin head domain (IBS1), and a second in the C-terminal rod region of talin (IBS2), mapped to the R11-R12 domains. Whilst the structural details of integrin binding to IBS1 are well understood, IBS2’s mode of binding integrin is less clear, and the biochemical details of this site have been elusive. Here we report that talin R11 contains a cryptic high affinity talin-binding site. We show that mechanical unfolding of R11 exposes an Aggregation Prone Region (APR) in Helix50 that oligomerizes with other talin R11s. Our data support a model whereby the process of mechanically unfolding one R11, exposes and maintains the APR in a high affinity conformation that drives unfolding of other R11 domains and oligomerisation. Atomic Force Microscopy confirms that the APR region alone forms micron long amyloid-like fibres, via a beta-sheet amyloid arrangement which can be abolished using a canonical “gatekeeper” point mutation, V2078K, that prevents APR interactions. Introducing this gatekeeper mutant in talin eliminates recruitment of talin IBS2 to integrin adhesion sites. The APR region in talin overlaps with a vinculin-binding site in Helix50, and we show a novel role for vinculin as a mechano-chaperone for talin, able to resolve the talin large species by binding to the VBS in Helix50. In light of this new information, we propose that the ability of R11-R12 to target to integrin adhesion complexes and enhance integrin activation can be better explained by a model where functional aggregation of talin serves to recruit and activate more talin molecules at the adhesion site leading to enhanced integrin activation. Whilst further work is required to fully exclude integrin binding to R11 we suggest that the name IBS2 might be a misnomer and propose the name Aggregation Prone Region 1 (APR1) for this talin oligomerisation motif.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: An aggregation-prone region in talin controls talin self-interactions and regulates integrin adhesion complex dynamics

abstract: Abstract Population structure and environmental features often capture major axes of genetic variation in many species. Yet the impacts of human activity often remain unquantified. For domesticated species that rely on human activity for survival and dispersal, human movements and cultural differences may play key roles patterning genetic diversity. Maize is a staple crop of enormous cultural importance to indigenous peoples of the Americas, but cannot survive or disperse without farmers. Using publicly available genotyping and passport data from approximately 2,000 traditional maize varieties, more than 500 whole genome sequences of humans from Mexico, and indigenous linguistic maps, we quantify anthropogenic effects on maize genetic diversity in the Americas. Maize shows very little overall structure, highlighting the effectiveness of indigenous farmers in moving and mixing maize populations. While principal components of maize diversity show meaningful correlations to human genetic diversity, our linear modeling suggests little additional impact of human population structure beyond shared geography. Though differences in maize diversity are often patterned by language locally, we find only weak genome-wide effects at larger spatial scales. Despite the relatively weak global signal of anthropogenic effects, linguistic GWAS, outlier F ST analyses, and selection scans identified loci associated with specific languages. Leveraging landscape-level sequencing data, we highlight how anthropogenic factors have shaped patterns of maize genetic diversity across Mesoamerica.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Maize genetic diversity is largely unstructured by human ethnolinguistic diversity in its center of origin

abstract: Decomposing virulence into host and pathogen effects is key to understanding how virulence is generated during infection, and how host and pathogen contributions evolve over time. Conventional virulence decomposition is, however, not designed to quantify how these contributions vary throughout an infection. Building on conventional virulence decomposition, we developed a dynamic framework that integrates disease space analysis to quantify these changing contributions. We applied this framework to existing data from house finches ( Haemorhous mexicanus ) experimentally infected with the emerging bacterial pathogen, Mycoplasma gallisepticum , examining two biologically meaningful infection phases: an early phase dominated by innate immune responses and a later phase in which the adaptive immune response is fully activated. Our analyses revealed that virulence components evolved differently across infection phases, with pathogen exploitation, per-parasite-pathogenicity (PPP), and host resistance each exhibiting distinct trajectories. These findings corroborated several known evolutionary patterns, while also revealing the evolution of increased PPP in this system. In contrast, the apparent evolution of host tolerance inferred from aggregated peak measurements was not supported by phase-specific analyses, demonstrating that aggregated and phase-specific measures can provide different mechanistic insights into virulence. By linking conventional virulence decomposition with disease space analysis, our dynamic virulence decomposition framework provides a general approach for quantifying how host and pathogen processes shape virulence over the course of infection.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Dynamic virulence decomposition disentangles host and pathogen contributions over the course of infection

abstract: Fertilization is a fundamental biological process that enables the fusion of a spermatozoon with an oocyte to initiate embryonic development. However, the underlying mechanisms leading to fertilization failure remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrated that the actin-related protein (Arp) family members ACTRT2 and ACTRT3 are essential for fertilization in both humans and mice, whereas ACTL10 is dispensable for fertility and the human-specific ACTL8 may play a role in early spermatogenesis. Ultrastructural and immunofluorescence analyses revealed that, during spermatogenesis, ACTRT2 or ACTRT3 deficiency disrupts the assembly of subacrosomal layer of the perinuclear theca (SAL-PT), leading to acrosome detachment and subsequent manchette abnormalities, which in turn impairs the formation of the postacrosomal sheath of the PT. These structural defects were accompanied by reduced abundance of the candidate sperm-borne oocyte-activating factors PAWP and PLCζ. Moreover, knockout of Actrt2 or Actrt3 severely impaired spermatozoa’s ability to penetrate the zona pellucida during in vitro fertilization. Mechanistically, ACTRT2, ACTRT3, ACTL7A, ACTL7B, and ACTL9 form a testis-enriched Arp complex in the SAL-PT and maintain the stability of one another. This complex interacts with the PT protein CAPZA3, which subsequently binds and stabilizes PLCζ. Additionally, the Arp complex interacts with DPY19L2/FAM209-associated proteins to mediate acrosome anchoring to the nuclear envelope. Therefore, these findings established a sequential DPY19L2/FAM209-associated protein–Arp complex–CAPZA3 scaffold extending from the nuclear envelope to the acrosome that is indispensable for fertilization. Collectively, we defined a previously unidentified structural and molecular framework for fertilization and provided insights into the diagnosis and treatment of fertilization failure.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: A DPY19L2/FAM209-associated protein–Arp complex–CAPZA3 scaffold is essential for perinuclear theca assembly and fertilization

abstract: Abstract Hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated 1 channels (HCN1) mediate the I h cationic current and play a central role in regulating neuronal excitability and synaptic integration. HCN1 is predominantly expressed in the neocortex and hippocampus. Pathogenic variants in HCN1 have been increasingly identified in individuals presenting with a broad spectrum of epileptic disorders, ranging from severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) to milder epilepsies. Here, we used patch-clamp electrophysiology in combination with confocal imaging in HEK293 cells to functionally characterize 43 HCN1 variants found in patients presenting with neurodevelopmental disorders, with or without epilepsy. Based on their biophysical properties, we defined four functional classes: (I) low or no current, (II) hyperpolarizing (i.e. left) shift in voltage dependence, (III) depolarizing (i.e. right) shift in voltage dependence, and (IV) generation of an instantaneous current. Integration of this functional classification with detailed clinical data from a cohort of 49 patients revealed a striking genotype-phenotype correlation. Loss-of-function variants were strongly enriched among individuals without epilepsy or with milder generalized phenotypes, whereas gain-of-function and mixed variants were predominantly associated with epilepsy, including all cases of DEE. Notably, non-epileptic cases clustered within a subgroup of loss-of-function variants affecting the selectivity filter. We further show that allosteric modulators, including the peptides NB6 and TRIP8b nano and the small molecule J&J12e, normalize the functional properties of mutant HCN1 channels in three classes. These findings establish a clinically relevant framework for interpreting HCN1 gain- and loss-of-function variants suggesting that the direction of channel dysfunction is a major determinant of epilepsy risk and severity.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Comprehensive classification of HCN1 variants linked to neurodevelopmental disorders with and without epilepsy

abstract: What drives exploration? Understanding the intrinsic motivation to explore is a long-standing challenge in both cognitive science and AI. In this study, we directly compare adults, children aged 8 to 12 y, and AI agents exploring a complex, open-ended environment called Crafter ( 1 ). We study how three common information-theoretic intrinsic objectives—entropy, information gain, and empowerment—relate to their behavior. We find that all three are positively correlated with human exploration progress for both children and adults, although entropy and empowerment are more strongly related to exploration progress in children than information gain. Furthermore, across agents and humans we observe that entropy initially increases rapidly, then plateaus, while empowerment increases continuously, suggesting that in early exploration they look for novel states, while in advanced exploration they look for states they can control. Finally, we find preliminary evidence that private speech about goals may aid exploration in children. Our data are available at https://github.com/alyd/humans_in_crafter_data .
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Intrinsically motivated humans and agents in open-world exploration

abstract: Lead (Pb) exposure remains a major environmental risk factor for cognitive dysfunction, yet the cellular mechanisms underlying Pb-induced memory impairment are poorly understood. Here, we show that both developmental and adult-onset Pb exposure selectively disrupts protein-synthesis-dependent long-term memory (LTM) in Drosophila melanogaster while sparing other memory forms. Using a mitochondria-targeted redox biosensor (mito-roGFP2-Orp1), we found that Pb elevates mitochondrial oxidative stress and disrupts redox homeostasis in cholinergic neurons and in dorsal-anterior-lateral (DAL) neurons, a critical locus for LTM consolidation. Pb-induced redox imbalance suppresses training-induced de novo protein synthesis in DAL neurons, thereby impairing memory consolidation. Antioxidant treatment with epigallocatechin gallate restores mitochondrial redox balance and rescues LTM by reinstating activity-dependent protein synthesis in DAL neurons. These findings identify mitochondrial redox dysregulation as a key mechanism linking environmental Pb exposure to impaired memory consolidation. Our results further establish a genetically tractable platform for dissecting neurotoxic mechanisms and for evaluating antioxidant-based strategies to mitigate Pb-induced cognitive dysfunction.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Lead impairs long-term memory by disrupting mitochondrial redox homeostasis in Drosophila

abstract: Wet age-related macular degeneration (AMD), a leading cause of irreversible vision loss, is driven by pathological choroidal neovascularization (CNV). Although anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapies remain the clinical standard, their utility is constrained by incomplete responses in nearly 50% of patients and off-target risks—such as geographic atrophy—stemming from non-specific VEGF blockade. Here, we identify a robust correlation between vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (VCAM-1) and VEGF/VEGF receptor (VEGFR) expression in aqueous humor from AMD patients and in murine CNV models. Thus, we engineered a tetravalent bispecific protein, RHV, by functionalizing an L-rhamnulose-1-phosphate aldolase scaffold with peptides that selectively bind VCAM-1 and the VEGFR on neovessels. The tetravalent design confers high apparent affinity, enhancing pathological endothelial targeting while sparing healthy retinal vasculature. RHV induces concurrent internalization and lysosomal degradation of both VCAM-1 and VEGFR via a head-to-tail binding mode, leading to sustained inhibition of the VEGF/VEGFR, PI3K/AKT and Apelin/APJ signaling pathways. In murine CNV models, a single intravitreal injection of RHV exhibits superior ocular retention and lesion penetration, achieving therapeutic efficacy comparable to aflibercept [a ligand-trap fusion protein for VEGF-A, VEGF-B and placental growth factor (PIGF)] at one-quarter of the molar dose. This dual-receptor degradation-based strategy represents a targeted and durable approach for treating ocular neovascularization.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: A tetravalent bispecific protein enables targeted degradation of VCAM-1 and VEGFR for treatment of choroidal neovascularization

abstract: Knots are common in long chains, from DNA and proteins to everyday strings, yet direct observation of knot dynamics is difficult. Using granular chains on vibrating platforms, we directly visualize knot dynamics and find that knot cores spontaneously tighten, a behavior observed across different knot types. We quantitatively explain spontaneous knot tightening using knot-tube theory: segments confined within the knot core experience entropic loss and tend to escape the core to gain conformational entropy. Although driven granular chains are not in thermodynamic equilibrium, their steady-state knot-size statistics are approximately captured by equilibrium statistical mechanics and Monte Carlo simulations. Analyses of state-transition probabilities and time-reversal asymmetry suggest a weak violation of detailed balance when the granular dynamics are projected onto the knot-size coordinate. Finally, we discuss the possible relevance of knot tightening to topoisomerase-mediated DNA unknotting.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Entropic tightening of knots in granular chains under vibration

abstract: Wastewater treatment greatly reduces mercury pollution in aquatic ecosystems but does not eliminate it. Here, we identify municipal sludge disposal as a major, long-overlooked atmospheric mercury source. In China, sludge disposal emitted 42 - 10 + 18 Mg in 2024, exceeding 10% of national anthropogenic emissions and ranking third after cement production and nonferrous metal smelting. These emissions have increased by nearly a thousandfold since the 1970s and are concentrated in densely populated urban areas, driven by the rapid expansion of sludge incineration, codisposal, and composting. Our findings reveal a cross-media pollution transfer embedded in sustainability transitions and call for sludge disposal to be incorporated into UNEP mercury budget and Minamata Convention assessments.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Municipal sludge disposal emerges as a major, hidden, and rapidly growing atmospheric mercury source

abstract: ABSTRACT The subependymal zone (SEZ) of the mammalian brain is the most active germinal area that continues to generate newborn neurons throughout life. This area harbors a population of neural stem cells (NSCs) that can be found in different states of activation, each differing in proliferative capacity and molecular signature: quiescent NSCs (qNSCs), primed NSCs (pNSCs), and activated NSCs (aNSCs). There is currently a void in terms of the specific markers available to effectively discern between these transient states. Likewise, the molecular signaling mechanisms controlling the transition from quiescence to activation remain largely unexplored, as do the factors influencing the decision between differentiation and self-renewal during NSC division. Here, we present evidence that the metabotropic P2Y 13 purinergic receptor plays a critical role in regulating adult neurogenesis. We found that P2Y 13 is specifically expressed in NSCs within the adult SEZ and that its levels can be used to distinguish qNSCs from aNSCs. Functionally, P2Y 13 signaling promotes NSC activation, enhancing lineage progression, while dampening their self-renewal capacity. Conversely, pharmacological blockade or genetic silencing of the P2Y 13 receptor favors NSC quiescence. Thus, we identified the metabotropic P2Y 13 purinergic receptor as a pivotal modulator of NSC dynamics, influencing both the balance between NSC quiescence and activation and the mode of NSC division at the subependymal zone.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: The purinergic receptor P2Y 13 controls the activation and mode of division of adult ventricular–subventricular zone neural stem cells

abstract: Between 2007 and 2020, implicit and explicit intergroup attitudes declined in bias steadily and were forecasted to continue toward attitude neutrality. But, since 2020, 5 y of new data (2021–2025) from 2.8 million U.S. respondents reveal that past trends have stalled or, in some cases, even reversed. The largest reversals in bias emerged for sexuality, transgender, race, and skin-tone bias which increased by 12 to 22% on implicit measures and by 24% to more than tripling on explicit measures. Age, disability, and body weight bias also increased, but at relatively slower rates. Breakpoint analyses showed that implicit attitudes were early indicators of change, reversing trend ~1 y earlier than explicit reports. For most topics, reversals were widespread across demographic groups and even extended to an international sample of 274,884 non-U.S. respondents. However, younger respondents (<20-y-old)—who had previously shown the largest decreases in bias—now showed the largest increases in bias; these trends also interacted with politics and gender (e.g., young conservative men were the most likely to increase). Exploratory analyses ruled out various single-cause explanations. Instead, we suggest that the best explanation is that 2020–2021 marked a turning point in the sociopolitical climate, whereby co-occurring existential threats from the COVID-19 pandemic, amplified economic insecurity, political sectarianism, and online toxicity prompted increases in intergroup bias. These data underscore how large populations of individual-level attitudes are continually shaped and altered by macro, societal-level events.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Patterns of implicit and explicit attitudes V: Increases in bias from 2021 to 2025

abstract: Metamaterials offer unprecedented control over physical fields through their microstructure, but current design methods cannot meet the demands of scenarios involving active sources, multiphysics field coupling, and multifunctional requirements. Moreover, existing approaches are generally developed for specific functions, making it difficult to integrate different functionalities and select the functional priorities within a single structure. To overcome these limitations, this study presents a systematic inverse design framework for multifunctional multiphysics metamaterials via multiobjective optimization. To uniformly explore the Pareto front, which clearly exhibits trade-offs among functionalities and facilitates the selection of functional priorities, we employ dynamic normalization into the decomposition-based multiobjective evolutionary algorithm. A robust anisotropic unit-cell database is constructed and used for generating metamaterials with optimized microstructures for multifunctionality. Three complex cases are studied that can simultaneously achieve mechanical cloaking plus stress minimization, thermal cloaking plus stress minimization, and direct current cloaking plus thermal stress minimization. Furthermore, the proposed framework is employed in potential engineering problems, for example, to realize mechanical cloaking by embedding functional components in structural materials, while minimizing the surrounding stress on functional components for mechanical protection when the assembled structures are compressed, thereby decoupling the interaction between functional and structural components. This systematic framework expands the capabilities of metamaterials in complex multiphysics coupling, offering a robust blueprint for future intelligent, structurally and functionally integrated systems.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Multifunctional multiphysics metamaterials via decomposition-based multiobjective optimization design

abstract: Abstract The Niemann-Pick Type C1-Related protein of the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum , PfNCR1, is a promising anti-malarial drug target facilitating cholesterol homeostasis at the interface of the malaria parasite with its host-red blood cell. PfNCR1 is localized to otherwise functionally uncharacterized regions covering ∼half of the host-parasite interface. These regions are defined by exceptionally narrow membrane contact sites, leaving only ∼3-4 nm vertical aqueous space in between the membranes. Determining the origin and functional consequence of localization to the closely apposed membrane is central for our understanding of PfNCR1 as drug target but also offers a window into the mechanism of the group of homologous proteins, associated with congenital conditions and cancer. Here we define the mechanism of PfNCR1’s membrane contact site localization and its implication for cholesterol transport. We identified a 141 amino acid long (amphipathic) helix - linker - (amphipathic) helix domain (“HLH domain”) unique to Plasmodium spp. , that is necessary for efficient localization of PfNCR1 to the narrow membrane contact sites. Mechanistically, we show that this localization relies on the HLH domain’s physicochemical properties. GPI-anchoring the isolated HLH domain or a version of the HLH domain in which the helices are replaced by the amphipathic helix of human ATG3 are sufficient to target a fluorescent protein to regions of endogenous PfNCR1. Functionally, we demonstrate that the degree of PfNCR1 localization to narrow contact sites qualitatively correlates with its ability to maintain cholesterol homeostasis, linking PfNCR1’s membrane contact to its recognized transport function. Collectively, the results establish the HLH domain as key element for PfNCR1’s localization and effectiveness in cholesterol transport while also opening avenues to probe the narrow membrane contact site regions with engineered proteins.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Amphipathic helices repurpose a Patched/NPC1-like cholesterol transporter to function at Plasmodium –erythrocyte membrane contact sites

abstract: Soil stores the largest pool of actively cycling carbon (C) on land, and its dynamics under global changes are critical for projecting climate feedbacks. Global nitrogen (N) deposition has more than doubled since the 1860s; however, the temporal dynamics of soil C emissions under prolonged N deposition are poorly understood. Here, using a global time-series dataset compiled from 38 long-term experiments in forests and grasslands, we find that the response of soil respiration (Rs) to N addition systematically shifts from a transient increase persisting for approximately 2 y to a sustained suppression over time (mean effect = −6%; 95% CI = [−10%, −3%]). Rs in forests and grasslands followed consistent nonlinear trajectories, characterized by a rapid initial decline in the magnitude of the response, which progressively leveled off. Notably, suppression of Rs emerged when cumulative N inputs exceeded a threshold of ~100 kg N ha −1 . Consequently, the suppression was both stronger and occurred more rapidly under high-level N additions (>50 kg N ha −1 y −1 ). These temporal dynamics were associated with N-induced soil acidification and related changes in microbial properties. Overall, these findings indicate that accurate prediction of land–atmosphere C fluxes under global change requires models to capture the reported temporal dynamics.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Progressive shifts in soil respiration response to long-term nitrogen enrichment across global forests and grasslands

abstract: Adaptive evolution associated with dispensable gene loss is widespread in the animal kingdom. However, loss of genes essential for embryonic survival and the mechanisms that evolved to bypass negative selection and extinction are less well known. Here, we show that all Gadiformes, an ecologically dominant order of codfishes, lost the aqp1ab -type genes that are essential for the formation of hydrated pelagic eggs and embryonic survival of marine teleosts in oceanic environments. Despite such gene loss, codfishes produce some of the most highly hydrated pelagic eggs of all marine teleosts. To resolve this apparent paradox, we initially confirmed that the mechanisms of osmotic drive are conserved with other pelagic-egg-producing marine teleosts, and then conducted comparative transcript analyses of aquaporin water channels in distantly-related freshwater and marine teleosts. This uncovered Aqp4-type channels that have been chromosomally linked to the Aqp1-type channels in jawed vertebrate genomes for >450 million years as the primary candidates. Using immunolocalization, functional assays, and inhibition experiments with zebrafish and Atlantic cod as model organisms, we show that short isoforms of Aqp4 are required for egg ovulation in more ancestral lineages of freshwater teleosts and were recruited to the oocyte hydration pathway of codfishes. By contrast, the oldest and most modern lineages of marine teleosts producing pelagic eggs still utilize the aqp1ab genes for egg hydration. Our data thus reveal that codfishes survived essential gene loss by functionally co-opting freshwater ovulatory pathways to marine egg hydration.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Codfishes survived essential gene loss by functionally co-opting freshwater ovulatory pathways to marine egg hydration

abstract: First proposed by Milgrom in 1983 as an alternative to the standard Cold Dark Matter (CDM) paradigm, Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND) has gained renewed momentum in light of persistent nondetections of exotic dark matter particles and growing tensions facing CDM on galactic scales. While MOND perfectly reproduces galactic rotation curves, it encounters notable challenges in explaining the equilibrium of galaxy clusters. Although it reduces the overall dark matter budget in these massive systems, an unidentified mass component remains required. This paper investigates the hypothesis that this missing mass is baryonic: composed of nonradiating ordinary matter such as stellar remnants, gas too diffuse to initiate star formation, or compact, ultra-dense clouds of cold molecular gas with low volume filling factors. Using a sample of 106 clusters mapped in X-rays, emitted by the hot intracluster medium composing most of the visible mass, we derive first the total mass within the Newtonian dynamics, assuming hydrostatic equilibrium and spherical symmetry. Then, with the modified Poisson equation, we reconstruct the spatial distribution of the invisible missing matter within the MOND framework. In the sample, the relaxed systems harboring cooling flows, known as cool-core clusters, have the highest peaks of dark missing mass. Its density profile reveals a pronounced central concentration bounded by a steep truncation immediately beyond a core radius of 20 to 30 kpc, confirming previous studies. MOND reduces the necessary dynamical mass by a factor of 4 to 10. The residual missing mass is proportional to the total gas mass, being roughly twice lower.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Modified Newtonian Dynamics and galaxy clusters

abstract: Françoise Combes’s childhood curiosity motivated her to pursue a career in science. Her studies in physics at the École Normale Supérieure in Paris eventually led her to focus on astrophysics. With help from mentors, such as astrophysicists Evry Schatzman and Pierre Encrenaz, Combes has had a distinguished career in astrophysics. She is renowned for her work studying the formation and evolution of galaxies and their dynamics and her research on dark matter. In her Inaugural Article, she describes her latest work exploring alternatives to dark matter.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Profile of Françoise Combes

abstract: General Relativity (GR) is an effective field theory valid in the infrared regime. Quadratic curvature extensions intended to probe ultraviolet physics generically propagate a massive spin-$2$ ghost and are therefore non-unitary. One route to remove ghost is by enlarging the geometric sector (torsion, non-metricity). We investigate the infrared phenomenology of both the standard (ghostful) and ghost-free fourth-order gravity theories by computing Gravitational Wave (GW) emission and confronting the results with observations such as the orbital-period decay of quasi-stable binaries such as PSR B1913+16 and PSR J1738+0333 and the chirp-mass evolution of GW170817. In the ghostful theory, besides the theoretical inconsistency due to non-unitarity, there are also phenomenological problems: the massless spin-$2$ GW flux cancels the combined GW fluxes of the massive spin-$2$ ghost and massive spin-$0$ scalar in the vanishing-mass limit, so the GR quadrupole formula is not recovered at the leading order. As a result, we obtain the GW constraint on the ghostful theory as $m\gtrsim 10^{-11}~\mathrm{eV}$, where $m$ is the mass of the massive modes. By contrast, the ghost-free theory smoothly reproduces the Newtonian potential and GR quadrupole formulae when the two coupling constants $α_1$ and $α_2$ vanish, independently of the mass $m$. Therefore, GW observations put mass-dependent upper bounds on the size of the coupling constants. For example, if we assume $α_1\simeqα_2$ for simplicity, then we obtain $α_{1,2}\lesssim 4.2\times 10^{83}$ for $m\sim 3\times 10^{-16}\,\mathrm{eV}$ and $α_{1,2}\lesssim 1.3\times 10^{75}$ for $m\sim 10^{-11}\,\mathrm{eV}$. To our knowledge, these are the first astrophysical-scale bounds reported for ghostful and ghost-free fourth-order gravity.
title: Exorcising ghosts with gravitational waves

abstract: Loop-current (LC) order and the associated time-reversal symmetry breaking (TRSB) are pivotal for understanding hidden magnetism and unconventional superconductivity in strongly correlated quantum materials. The recently discovered kagome metal CsV$_3$Sb$_5$ provides a unique platform for exploring these intertwined phenomena. In this study, we utilize $^{121}$Sb nuclear quadrupole resonance (NQR) and $^{51}$V nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) measurements to investigate the possible existence of the LC order in CsV$_3$Sb$_5$. Below $T^\ast \approx 45$ K, we observe a field-independent NMR linewidth broadening at the V site in a high-quality single crystal, which indicates an internal magnetic field of 3.6 Oe at the V position. We show that this internal field arises from a static LC state that produces orbital magnetic moments $μ_{\rm orb}$ ranging from 0.002 to 0.01 $μ_B$. Detailed analysis suggests that the observed LC state breaks $C_6$ rotational symmetry to possess a low symmetry of $C_2$. Our results provide microscopic evidence for LC order in the charge density wave (CDW) phase of CsV$_3$Sb$_5$ and show that TRSB is intertwined with electronic nematicity, imposing stringent constraints on microscopic descriptions of the kagome CDW and its relation to superconductivity.
title: NMR evidence for a loop-current state with broken C 6 symmetry in the charge-ordered CsV 3 Sb 5

abstract: We provide a cluster algebraic construction of the cube root symbol letters that appear at leading order in the near-collinear expansion of the four-point energy correlator in $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM theory.
title: Cluster algebras, cube roots, and energy correlators in 𝒩 = 4 super Yang-Mills theory

abstract: We report the first measurement of the semileptonic decay $D^+_s \rightarrow K^*(892)^0μ^+ν_μ$ and an improved measurement of the decay $D^+_s \rightarrow K^*(892)^0 e^+ν_{e}$ using a sample of $7.33~\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$ of $e^+e^-$ annihilation data collected at center-of-mass energies between 4.128 to 4.226~GeV with the BESIII detector at the BEPCII collider. We measure the branching fractions to be $\mathcal B({D^+_s\rightarrow K^*(892)^0 μ^+ν_μ})=(2.07\pm0.22_{\rm stat}\pm0.10_{\rm syst})\times10^{-3}$ and $\mathcal B({D^+_s\rightarrow K^*(892)^0 e^+ν_{e}})=(2.14\pm0.18_{\rm stat}\pm0.10_{\rm syst})\times10^{-3}$. Based on a simultaneous study of the dynamics in two semileptonic decays, the hadronic form factor parameters in the $D^+_s\rightarrow K^{*}(892)^0$ transition are determined to be $r_{V} = V(0)/A_1(0) = 1.63 \pm 0.14_{\rm stat} \pm 0.08_{\rm syst}$, $r_{2} = A_2(0)/A_1(0) = 0.60 \pm 0.13_{\rm stat} \pm 0.06_{\rm syst}$, and $A_1(0)=0.56 \pm 0.02_{\rm stat} \pm 0.01_{\rm syst}$, where $V(0)$ is the vector form factor and $A_{1,2}(0)$ are the axial-vector form factors evaluated at $q^2=0$. The precision of $r_V$ and $r_2$ is improved by twofold and $A_1(0)$ is measured for the first time. We also report the first model-independent measurements of the differential decay rates and the lepton forward-backward asymmetries for $D^+_s\rightarrow K^{*}(892)^0\ell^+ν_{\ell}$ decays. Based on these measurements, we perform a test of lepton flavor universality in full and separate $q^2$ intervals with $D^+_s\rightarrow K^{*}(892)^0\ell^+ν_{\ell}$ decays. No violation is found within uncertainties. Our results present for the first time a complete study of the dynamics in the $D_s^+\rightarrow K^*(892)^0$ transition, and provide stringent tests of various non-perturbative theoretical calculations.
title: First measurement of the D s + → K * ( 892 ) 0 μ + ν μ decay, study of dynamics and test of lepton universality with D s + → K * ( 892 ) 0 ℓ + ν ℓ decays

abstract: In the ultrastrong light-matter coupling regime, the ability to confine the electric field to subwavelength scales and define an electromagnetic mode is essential. This task is typically achieved through dedicated cavities, such as THz metal resonators. Here, we instead introduce ultrastrong coupling directly between distinct magnetoplasmon excitations, leveraging solely the spatial symmetry of a confined electronic medium in the presence of a magnetic field. By patterning an AlGaN/GaN single quantum well hosting a two-dimensional electron gas into micrometer-scale patches, we tailor the mutual interactions between topologically protected edge and bulk magnetoplasmons, achieving coupling strengths of up to 0.1. The progressive breaking of rotational symmetry determines the coupling rules and leads to the emergence of energy gaps and unique chiral-mode hybridization. Our results highlight a path towards exploiting the symmetry class and topology of the magnetoplasmon wavefunction as a new parameter space for ultrastrong light-matter interaction without a dedicated cavity.
title: Ultrastrong coupling of topologically protected edge and bulk magnetoplasmons

abstract: The Schrödinger wavefunction is ubiquitous in quantum mechanics, quantum chemistry, and bosonic quantum information theory. Its zero-set for fermionic systems is well-studied and central for determining chemical properties, yet for bosonic systems the zero-set is less understood, especially in the context of characterizing non-classicality. Here we study the zeros of such wavefunctions and give them a novel information-theoretic interpretation. Our main technical result is showing that the wavefunction of most bosonic quantum systems can be extended to a holomorphic function over the complex plane, allowing the application of powerful techniques from complex analysis. As a consequence, we prove a version of Hudson's theorem for the wavefunction and characterize Gaussian dynamics as classical motion of the wavefunction zeros. Our findings suggest that the non-Gaussianity of quantum optical states can be detected by measuring a single quadrature of the electromagnetic field, which we demonstrate in a companion paper [arXiv:2507.23005]. More generally, our results show that the non-Gaussian features of bosonic quantum systems are encoded in the zeros of their wavefunction.
title: Complex zeros of the wavefunction
